subject: English
passage: In the 1980s and '90s, fish farmers developed smaller varieties of salmon and trout with faster growth rates. Marine biologist Cristina Enescu, Demetrius Byrd, and other aquaculture specialists are building on that work by exploring the development of smaller tuna varieties. Larger size can allow individual fish to produce more offspring per spawning cycle. However, larger size also makes the fish more vulnerable to predators and diseases before they reach maturity. Because of this trade-off, some aquaculture specialists suggest that smaller tuna varieties will actually ______
prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: be more vulnerable to predators due to their reduced ability to escape quickly.
choices.B: help improve reproduction rates by being more likely to survive to maturity despite producing fewer offspring per cycle.
choices.C: require more space in breeding facilities than small varieties of salmon and trout typically do.
choices.D: begin producing more offspring per spawning cycle than the largest variety of tuna currently does.

explanation:
Choice B is the best answer because it presents the conclusion that most logically completes the text's discussion about a trade-off in developing smaller varieties of tuna. The text explains that aquaculture specialists are working to develop smaller tuna varieties in an effort to improve reproduction rates. The text points out that although larger size in tuna can lead to more offspring per spawning cycle, it also makes the fish more vulnerable to predators and diseases before they reach maturity. This presents a clear trade-off between potential reproductive output (larger fish producing more offspring per cycle) and survival reliability (smaller fish surviving to reproductive maturity). Given this information, it is reasonable to infer that smaller tuna varieties, while possibly producing fewer offspring per cycle, would be more likely to survive until they can reproduce. This survival advantage would result in improved overall reproduction rates because more fish would reach maturity, thus offsetting the potential reduction in offspring per smaller fish.

Why A is incorrect:

Choice A is incorrect. According to the text, larger size makes tuna vulnerable to predators and diseases, implying that larger fish—not smaller ones—have greater vulnerability problems. The text provides no basis for inferring that smaller tuna varieties would be more vulnerable to predators; in fact, the text suggests the opposite relationship between size and vulnerability.
